messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi, a 25-year-old journalist, presented as a man hollowed out by fear. Six months prior, he and his best friend, Jamal, were covering a community vigil that devolved into a chaotic and violent police crackdown. He remembers the sudden panic, the jarring sound of a protest anthem abruptly cut off by shouting, and the rhythmic, heavy thud of boots on pavement closing in. He remembers seeing Jamal fall and the sharp, metallic sound that accompanied it. That night, a specific hip-hop track had been drifting from a nearby apartment window, a song Jamal loved, and now the memory of its bassline is inseparable from the auditory recall of sirens and his own ragged breathing.

In the weeks that followed, the event replayed not as a coherent story but as a series of sensory assaults. The memories feel more real to him than his present reality; the sound of footsteps behind him on the street is not just a sound but the direct, auditory recall of the officers approaching that night. These memory fragments are so vivid and intrusive they convince him the danger has never passed, leaving him in a constant state of high alert. This sense of ever-present threat makes it impossible for him to narrate the events clearly; when he tries, he loses the thread, overwhelmed by the sensory data. The sheer horror of these recurring experiences has led him to a devastating conclusion: his life has been destroyed by the trauma. He believes the happy, ambitious person he was before that night is gone forever. The memories themselves have become so painful that their mere presence in his mind acts as a trigger, a fresh reminder of his own terror and loss.

The world outside his apartment has since become a minefield of these triggers. A news report on his laptop about an unrelated police incident, the sound of footsteps from the apartment above, or hearing that specific song from a passing car—each cue instantly reactivates the terror. When triggered, he is plunged back into the most terrifying moments of the memory, feeling the same visceral fear as if it were happening all over again. This constant bombardment of threat reinforces his core belief that he is no longer the capable man he once was. In response to these triggers, he has developed a rigid set of protective behaviours. He avoids anything that reminds him of Jamal, which now includes their favourite restaurants and even mutual friends. He has started wearing hoodies and hats, even indoors, in an effort to become less noticeable, to conceal himself from a threat he feels is always watching.

This profound sense of being unsafe has dismantled his life piece by piece. His difficulty concentrating means he can stare at a blank page for hours, the words refusing to come, making his career as a journalist feel like a distant dream. This hypervigilance makes him scan his environment constantly, which in turn makes him more likely to notice potential triggers, tightening the loop of his anxiety. The exhaustion from this state of threat only makes the intrusive, vivid memories more frequent and harder to dismiss. This relentless cycle serves as daily confirmation of his most painful beliefs about himself: that he is broken and his life is ruined. He had come to believe he was no longer capable of doing the things that once defined him, and this conviction fuels both his sense of ambient threat and his retreat from the world. He avoids anything that might provoke a strong feeling, positive or negative, believing he can’t handle it. This appraisal also colours his memory, making it almost impossible to recall any aspect of his life with Jamal that isn't now tainted by the horror of its end.

His strategies for survival have become a cage. The more he avoids unfamiliar places or conceals himself in baggy clothing, the more his world shrinks, and the more isolated he feels. This isolation provides stark, daily proof for his belief that he is miserable and alone, a ghost in his own life. By trying to avoid all external reminders, he has inadvertently made himself more sensitive and reactive to the few that inevitably break through his defences. The perpetual sense of threat has made these behaviours feel not like choices but necessities; he feels compelled to check over his shoulder and avoid any place where he cannot immediately assess the danger.

Kofi finally sought therapy at the urging of his partner, who told him, “I feel like I’m living with a stranger.” He confessed that he agreed with her. He is trapped in a present that feels less real than his past, unable to work, unable to connect, and unable to feel anything but a pervasive sense of dread. He knows his life has been shattered, and what frightens him most is the thought that it can never be put back together.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not describe a direct causal link where triggers or reminders reinforce the patient's negative beliefs about himself or the world.
